thing: Tetraethyl lead (TEL) added to gasoline as an anti-knock agent
claim: Leaded exhaust would slowly poison the general public through chronic low-level lead absorption along roads, not just factory workers.
what_happened: TEL was sold for ~70 years; lead became a global contaminant linked to IQ loss and neurological harm; US phased it out 1976-1996 and the last country stopped in 2021.
dismissed_by: GM, DuPont and Ethyl Corp, an industry-funded Bureau of Mines study, Robert Kehoe, and the 1925 Surgeon General's conference which reached no conclusion
cost_of_error: An estimated 15+ million tonnes of lead released to the atmosphere; a 2011 estimate put the worldwide annual toll at 322 million lost IQ points and ~$2.4 trillion (4% of world GDP) per year.
lesson: When the warning is about slow, diffuse, low-dose exposure and the only safety data comes from the seller, assume the acute-incident framing is hiding the real risk.

quotes.text: probably the greatest single question in the field of public health that has ever faced the American public
quotes.speaker: Yandell Henderson
quotes.publication: The Nation (Jamie Lincoln Kitman, 'The Secret History of Lead', 2000)

quotes.text: and had failed even to take into account the possibility that the atmosphere might be polluted to such an extent along automobile thoroughfares that those who worked or lived along such streets would gradually absorb lead in sufficient quantities to poison them in the course of months
quotes.speaker: Yandell Henderson
quotes.publication: The Nation (Jamie Lincoln Kitman, 'The Secret History of Lead', 2000)

thing: Industrial asbestos in insulation, textiles, building products and brakes
claim: Asbestos dust carries easily demonstrated health risks to the people who work with it.
what_happened: Asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma were confirmed over the following decades; Johns-Manville had internal reports of worker deaths by 1930; most rich countries banned asbestos and the US EPA banned chrysotile in 2024.
dismissed_by: Asbestos manufacturers led by Johns-Manville, who kept diagnoses from workers and in 1951 removed references to cancer from funded research
cost_of_error: US asbestos litigation estimated at over $250 billion, the longest and most expensive mass tort in US history; dozens of manufacturers bankrupt since 1981; UK asbestos deaths in 2011 (4,721) exceeded all transport deaths.
lesson: A product whose harm shows up decades after exposure can be sold for generations after the first credible warning, so latency is a reason to act early, not to wait for proof.

quotes.text: Medical men in areas where asbestos is manufactured have long suspected the dust to be the cause of chronic bronchitis and fibrosis ...
quotes.speaker: W. E. Cooke
quotes.publication: Wikipedia, Health impact of asbestos (citing Cooke, British Medical Journal 1924)

quotes.text: It is now known that asbestos dust is one of the most dangerous dusts to which man is exposed.
quotes.speaker: U.S. Bureau of Mines (letter to Eagle-Picher)

thing: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs/Freon) in aerosol cans, refrigeration and foams
claim: CFCs released at ground level would drift to the stratosphere and destroy the ozone layer that screens UV radiation.
what_happened: The 1985 British Antarctic Survey paper revealed an Antarctic ozone hole with losses up to 70%, larger than predicted; the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs and Molina, Rowland and Crutzen won the 1995 Nobel Prize.
dismissed_by: DuPont's board chair ('a science fiction tale ... a load of rubbish') and the aerosol and halocarbon industries
cost_of_error: A 1986 EPA study projected an additional 40 million skin cancer cases and 800,000 cancer deaths in the US over 88 years absent controls; Antarctic ozone remained 40-50% below pre-hole levels into the 2010s.
lesson: A mechanism worked out in the lab can be right a decade before the field data arrives, and the fix happened only once the incumbent saw a substitute it could sell.

quotes.text: Mario and I realized that this was not just a scientific question, challenging and interesting to us, but a potentially grave environmental problem involving substantial depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer.
quotes.speaker: F. Sherwood Rowland

quotes.text: a science fiction tale ... a load of rubbish ... utter nonsense
quotes.speaker: Chair of the Board of DuPont (dismissal)

thing: DDT and other synthetic pesticides sprayed at mass scale
claim: Indiscriminate pesticide spraying bioaccumulates up the food chain, kills wildlife, threatens human health and breeds insect resistance.
what_happened: Eggshell thinning nearly wiped out bald eagles and peregrines and resistance undercut mosquito control, so the US banned agricultural DDT in 1972 and Stockholm banned it worldwide in 2004; human cancer harm stayed less clear and DDT is still allowed for indoor malaria control.
dismissed_by: American Cyanamid's Robert White-Stevens, Monsanto (parody 'The Desolate Year'), former Agriculture Secretary Ezra Taft Benson, the USDA
cost_of_error: More than 600,000 tonnes applied in the US before the 1972 ban; bald eagle and peregrine falcon pushed to near-extinction in the contiguous US; agricultural overuse created the resistance that weakened DDT against malaria.
lesson: Carson was right about ecology and resistance and is still contested on human health, so it pays to separate the parts of a warning that hold up from the parts that may not.

quotes.text: No responsible person contends that insect-borne disease should be ignored. The question that has now urgently presented itself is whether it is either wise or responsible to attack the problem by methods that are rapidly making it worse.
quotes.speaker: Rachel Carson
quotes.publication: Silent Spring, quoted in Wikipedia, Silent Spring

quotes.text: If man were to follow the teachings of Miss Carson, we would return to the Dark Ages, and the insects and diseases and vermin would once again inherit the earth
quotes.speaker: Robert White-Stevens, American Cyanamid (dismissal)

thing: PFOA (C8), the 'forever chemical' used to make Teflon and other fluoropolymers
claim: DuPont's own toxicologists found C8 was toxic, enlarged animal organs and should be handled with extreme care.
what_happened: DuPont kept using and releasing C8 for decades; a court-ordered science panel found 'probable links' to kidney and testicular cancer, thyroid disease and more; PFOA was phased out and EPA set an enforceable 4.0 ppt drinking-water limit in April 2024.
dismissed_by: DuPont and 3M management, who kept the studies internal while PFOA products earned about $1 billion a year in profit
cost_of_error: 1.7 million pounds of C8 released from the Parkersburg plant 1951-2003; 99.7% of Americans had detectable PFOA in 2003-04; DuPont/Chemours paid a $670.7 million settlement in 2017 over 3,550 injury suits plus $16.5 million to EPA in 2005.
lesson: When a company's own lab flags a persistent chemical early and the product is a profit pillar, expect the warning to stay internal until litigation forces discovery.

quotes.text: available practical steps be taken to reduce that exposure.
quotes.speaker: Bruce Karrh, DuPont corporate medical director

claim: Lead paint poisons not just the painters but the people who live in houses painted with it.
what_happened: European countries restricted lead paint and the League of Nations recommended an interior ban in the early 1920s, but the US declined and only banned residential lead paint in 1978; paint chips and dust in pre-1978 homes remain a leading source of child lead exposure.
dismissed_by: The US lead industry (National Lead and peers) and the US government, which declined to adopt the League of Nations resolution
cost_of_error: US homes kept getting lead paint for 56 years after the League of Nations recommendation; pre-1978 housing is still a main source of childhood lead poisoning, which causes nervous system damage, stunted growth and kidney damage.
lesson: When peer countries have already restricted a product on health grounds, a domestic industry's resistance is not evidence of safety, just a lag.

quotes.text: poisonous in a large degree, both for the workmen and for the inhabitants of a house painted with lead colors
quotes.speaker: French expert, reported by Sherwin-Williams
quotes.publication: Wikipedia, Lead paint (citing Sherwin-Williams monthly, July 1904)

quotes.text: The following year, the League of Nations would recommend banning white-lead paints for interior use on health grounds, as many European countries had already done. Establishing a pattern of tolerance for this most dangerous element, the United States declined to adopt the league’s resolution.
quotes.speaker: Jamie Lincoln Kitman (historian narrative)

thing: Large-scale fossil fuel combustion and its CO2 emissions
claim: CO2 from burning fossil fuels would warm the planet, leaving a window of only five to ten years before hard decisions on energy strategy became critical.
what_happened: Exxon's own scientists projected warming of about 0.20C per decade, which matched later observations; the company cut its CO2 research in the late 1980s and funded public doubt while warming proceeded as predicted.
dismissed_by: Exxon management and the fossil fuel industry's lobbying and public relations campaigns of the 1980s-2000s
cost_of_error: A 2023 Science review found 63-83% of Exxon's private projections accurate; the decades of delay locked in roughly 1.1C of warming above pre-industrial levels by the 2010s.
lesson: When a company's own scientists' forecasts later prove accurate and its public messaging contradicts them, trust the internal model over the press release.

quotes.text: In the first place, there is general scientific agreement that the most likely manner in which mankind is influencing the global climate is through carbon dioxide release from the burning of fossil fuels,
quotes.speaker: James F. Black, Exxon senior scientist

quotes.text: holds that man has a time window of five to ten years before the need for hard decisions regarding changes in energy strategies might become critical.
quotes.speaker: James F. Black, Exxon senior scientist

thing: Tall-stack coal power plants and industrial sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions
claim: Sulfur and nitrogen emissions from distant smokestacks were acidifying rain and damaging lakes, soils and forests across borders.
what_happened: Hubbard Brook measured rain at pH 4.03 in 1972; the 1991 NAPAP assessment confirmed acidified lakes, lost trout habitat, soil and monument damage; the 1990 Clean Air Act Title IV cap-and-trade cut power-plant SO2 by about 10 million tons (~50%).
dismissed_by: The Reagan White House, Fred Singer's doubt-casting review of the 1983 Nierenberg panel draft, and the House, which voted down sulfur controls in 1983
cost_of_error: NAPAP 1991 found 5% of New England lakes acidic and 2% unable to support brook trout; controls were delayed about two decades after the Swedish and US warnings.
lesson: Pollution that crosses a border from the emitter to someone else gets dismissed longest, and a cheap market fix can exist well before politics allows it.

quotes.text: the precipitation over Sweden as a whole is definitely more acid than the CO2 equilibrium alone would permit
quotes.speaker: Two Swedish scientists (1955)

thing: Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant's tsunami design basis (5.7 m seawall-era assumptions, basement diesel generators)
claim: A tsunami far higher than TEPCO's design basis, up to 15.7 m, could hit the plant, as the 869 Jogan tsunami deposits showed.
what_happened: TEPCO's own 2008 simulation confirmed the risk but was not acted on and reached NISA only on 7 March 2011; four days later a 13-14 m tsunami overtopped the seawall, flooded the generators and caused three meltdowns.
dismissed_by: TEPCO and Japan's regulator NISA, which kept a 5.6 m forecast and set aside the Jogan evidence raised in 2009
cost_of_error: Japan's trade ministry estimated cleanup and compensation at 20 trillion yen (~$180 billion) in 2016; large areas were made uninhabitable for years.
lesson: Design for the worst event in the geological record, not the worst in living memory, and treat an internal study that contradicts the design basis as an emergency.

thing: Chisso Corporation's acetaldehyde plant discharging methylmercury wastewater into Minamata Bay
claim: The neurological epidemic in Minamata was organic mercury poisoning from Chisso's factory wastewater, accumulating in the fish people ate.
what_happened: Kumamoto University researchers named organic mercury in 1959 and Chisso's own hospital director reproduced the disease in cat 400 the same year, but Chisso hid the result, stopped his research and kept discharging until 1968, when the government officially recognised the cause.
dismissed_by: Chisso, the Ministry of International Trade and Industry and the Japan Chemical Industry Association, which funded rival theories
cost_of_error: 2,265 people officially recognised as victims by 2001 and over 10,000 compensated; Chisso had paid $86 million by 2004; a second outbreak hit Niigata in 1965.
lesson: When the polluter's own scientist confirms the harm and is told to stop, the company's funded counter-theories are a delay tactic, not a scientific dispute.

thing: Building a school and homes on Hooker Chemical's buried chemical waste landfill in Niagara Falls
claim: The buried chemical waste made the land unsafe to build on where underground work was needed and would harm anyone who lived over it.
what_happened: Chemicals seeped into basements; New York evacuated families in 1978 and the site became a Superfund cleanup lasting to 2004; studies found more low birth weight babies and birth defects, but the more dramatic chromosome and cancer claims were not consistently replicated.
dismissed_by: The Niagara Falls School Board, which built the school and sold the remaining land for housing, then Hooker/Occidental and officials who said residents' illnesses were unrelated
cost_of_error: Occidental paid $129 million to the EPA in 1995 after a court found Hooker negligent; a neighbourhood was demolished and the cleanup took 21 years, leading to the 1980 Superfund law.
lesson: A seller who adds liability waivers to a deed is telling you the risk is real, even when the size of the health harm is later disputed.

quotes.text: in view of the nature of the property and the purposes for which it has been used, it will be necessary for us to have special provisions incorporated into the deed with respect to the use of the property and other pertinent matters.
quotes.speaker: Hooker Chemical Company, letter to the Niagara Falls School Board

thing: BP's Macondo deepwater well cement job and temporary abandonment plan on the Deepwater Horizon rig
claim: With so few centralizers and a single casing string the cement job was likely to fail and the well would have a severe gas flow problem.
what_happened: BP ran the casing with six centralizers and skipped a cement bond log; on 20 April 2010 gas came up through the failed cement barrier, the rig exploded and sank, and the well spilled oil for 87 days.
dismissed_by: BP drilling managers, under schedule pressure with the well five weeks late, who chose fewer centralizers and overrode staff requests to re-squeeze
cost_of_error: 11 workers killed and 17 injured; the largest accidental marine oil spill in history; BP's total costs reached about $65 billion by 2018.
lesson: When a contractor's model says SEVERE and the team's reply is 'will probably be fine', the schedule has overruled the engineering, and the people closest to the work should be able to stop the job.

quotes.text: well is considered to have a SEVERE gas flow problem.
quotes.speaker: Jesse Gagliano, Halliburton cementing design report
quotes.publication: CBS News (quoting House Energy and Commerce Committee letter to Tony Hayward, June 2010)

quotes.text: Cement simulations indicate it is unlikely to be a successful cement job.
quotes.speaker: BP mid-April 2010 plan review
quotes.publication: CBS News (quoting House Energy and Commerce Committee letter to Tony Hayward, June 2010)

quotes.text: But, who cares, it's done, end of story, will probably be fine and we'll get a good cement job.
quotes.speaker: Brett Cocales, BP operations drilling engineer (dismissal)

thing: Bisphenol A (BPA) in polycarbonate bottles, food-can linings and receipts
claim: BPA acts as an endocrine disruptor at low, everyday doses well below the official safe level, with infants most at risk.
what_happened: The US, Canada and EU banned BPA in baby bottles as a precaution; EFSA's 2023 re-evaluation called for a much lower tolerable daily intake and the EU banned BPA in all food-contact materials in December 2024, while the US FDA still says BPA is safe at current levels.
dismissed_by: The chemical and plastics industry and the US FDA, which maintains BPA is safe at current food exposure levels
cost_of_error: Exposure was effectively lifelong across whole populations for decades; regulators on the two sides of the Atlantic still disagree on the size of the harm.
lesson: For a chemical that everyone is exposed to at low doses, regulators can split for decades, so build products that will survive the stricter regulator's ruling.

thing: Soviet RBMK graphite-moderated reactor design (positive void coefficient, graphite-tipped control rods)
claim: Inserting the RBMK's control rods from fully withdrawn could briefly add reactivity at the core bottom instead of shutting the reactor down.
what_happened: The positive scram effect found at Ignalina in 1983 was circulated, but the promised rod redesign and withdrawal limits were never imposed; on 26 April 1986 the scram at Chernobyl Unit 4 added reactivity and the reactor exploded.
dismissed_by: The RBMK Chief Design Engineer (NIKIET) and Soviet nuclear authorities, who said design changes would follow but made none
cost_of_error: Deaths from acute radiation sickness plus 15 fatal thyroid cancers, with long-term death estimates of up to 4,000 (UN) to 16,000 across Europe; about 350,000 people permanently resettled.
lesson: A known flaw that is noted and circulated but never fixed in hardware is not mitigated, and safety bulletins without follow-up are paperwork.

quotes.text: This latter effect was a result of faulty design of the rods, the nature of which had been discovered at the Ignalina nuclear power plant in 1983. However, no correction was made following this discovery at Ignalina, no compensatory measures were taken and any dissemination of information to operating organizations was not followed up.
quotes.speaker: IAEA International Nuclear Safety Advisory Group (INSAG-7)
quotes.publication: INSAG-7, The Chernobyl Accident: Updating of INSAG-1, IAEA Safety Series No. 75
